text: Course five showed Script Includes at an introductory level — mostly as a named container for a function or two, enough to get something working. Here's the real, standard pattern production ServiceNow developers actually write for almost every Script Include on a real instance: a full class-based structure built on four specific, deliberate pieces.

Here's IncidentUtils, built from those four pieces. Class.create assigns a constructor to the variable. The prototype is an object literal listing every method the class has: initialize sets a default priorityThreshold of two, meaning Critical or High, and isHighPriority compares a given record's priority field against that threshold, parsing it as an integer first. The trailing type property names the class as a plain string, IncidentUtils, matching the variable name exactly, character for character.

A caller uses it exactly like any other JavaScript object. New IncidentUtils constructs the instance, which immediately runs initialize behind the scenes and sets priorityThreshold before anything else in the class gets a chance to run. Then isHighPriority is called against the current record, and if that returns true, a work note gets added flagging it as high priority right at creation time.

Four pieces, four distinct jobs. Class.create is a real platform API, not a convention, and it returns an actual constructor function. The prototype object lists every method in one single place, reading closer to classical, Java-style object orientation than scattered, one-at-a-time prototype assignments would. Initialize is the constructor — it runs automatically and immediately at construction time, never waiting for the first method call. And type is required, not decorative: it's a string the platform's own internal reflection genuinely relies on, and letting it quietly drift out of sync with the actual class name after a rename is a real, surprisingly common bug on live instances.

Class.create, prototype, initialize, and type — that's the complete pattern, and you'll see it in almost every serious Script Include you ever open. Next, Lesson 13 covers real inheritance between Script Include classes, and exactly when extending one genuinely makes sense versus writing a brand-new class from scratch.
